newsitem.title: CYPRUS: EU appeals to Turkish Cypriots to end isolation.
newsitem.headline: EU appeals to Turkish Cypriots to end isolation.

text.p: The European Union appealed on Friday to Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash to bring his community out of "isolation" and move towards solving the protracted Cyprus dispute splitting the island for decades.

EU External Affairs Commissioner Hans Van Den Broek made his appeal after ending a round of talks on both sides of the eastern Mediterranean island, partitioned between the Turkish and Greek Cypriot communities since 1974.

"Mr. Denktash, please bring your community out of isolation, out of exile. Don't ask from us to recognise the independent state of Northern Cyprus. Nobody in the world does that except Turkey, and we want to abide by the rules, we want to abide by U.N. resolutions," van den Broek told Greek and Turkish Cypriot journalists at the Ledra Palace, a bullet-riddled hotel in the United-Nations controlled buffer zone splitting Nicosia.
The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government is due to start accession talks with the EU bloc next year.

Van den Broek told a news conference that the traditionally close ties Turkish Cypriots have with Turkey and fears expressed of losing their identity to the larger Greek Cypriot community could not be jeopardised by Cyprus's accession to the union.
Turkey invaded northern Cyprus in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling Greece at the time.
It is still unclear how Cyprus could become a member of the EU if by the end of a successful round of negotiations the division between the communities still remains.

"The European Union as a whole would like to see that circumstances and progress towards political settlement would permit an involvement of both communities in the accession talks," Van den Broek said.
The European official said Turkish Cypriots were entitled to their own cultural identity, an identity which he said he did not think "their southern Greek Cypriot compatriots" denied.
He said security concerns of the community could be addressed in the political settlement without being incompatible with EU membership.

Turkish Cypriots object to Cypriot membership of the union on grounds that international conventions do not permit the island to be a member of a body that Turkey -- a guarantor power with Britain and Greece -- is not a member of.
The conventions do not prevent Cyprus from becoming a member of the union in circumstances where Turkey has not joined it yet, an EU press release issued after the news conference said.
International mediators have recently stepped up efforts to solve the Cyprus dispute which sours relations between Greece and Turkey, both seen as the "motherlands" of each community.

Tension has been running high on the island since killings on both sides of the ceasefire line last year, a Greek Cypriot decision to purchase anti-aircraft missiles from Russia and warnings from Turkey, which has 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus, of a military strike to knock them out.
A solution, under a federal umbrella as defined by high level agreements between the two sides, could pave the way for smoother accession talks with Europe, van den Broek said.

He said the EU would be willing to approve exemptions from certain EU laws for Cyprus in a transitional period to allow for freedom of movement, free establishment and acquisition of property in the event of a political settlement.
Greece, and to a lesser extent the Greek Cypriots, reacted angrily to suggestions earlier this week to include the Turkish Cypriots, in an undefined capacity, in negotiations.
Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said this week Greece may respond by blocking the EU's enlargement.
"Theo Pangalos is a good friend but I didn't learn political sophistication from him," van den Broek.
